title: The Ball Poem
book: NCERT First Flight: Textbook in English for Class X
subject: english_literature
author: John Berryman
syllabus_note: CBSE 2025-26 English Language and Literature (184): First Flight poem 5. Assessed through poetry extracts (5 marks) and short answers (3 marks). Only short lines are quoted here; read the full poem in the NCERT textbook.

sections.title: A small loss, a big lesson

blocks.title: It was only a ball, or was it?
blocks.body: A boy's ball bounces down the street and falls into the harbour. An adult watching could easily buy him another one. But the poet chooses **not to**. Why? Because the boy is learning one of life's hardest lessons: **how to bear loss**.

blocks.title: The poet
blocks.body: **John Berryman** was an American poet, a Pulitzer Prize winner, known for poems about inner feelings and suffering. The Ball Poem shows how a small event in childhood can hold a big truth.
blocks.future: Psychologists, teachers and parents help children deal with loss; this poem shows why that matters.

blocks.question: Why does the poet not offer to buy the boy a new ball?
options: The boy must learn to accept loss; a new ball cannot replace what he has lost

blocks.title: What the poem says
blocks.body:
**The loss:** the poet asks, 'What is the boy now, who has lost his ball, / What, what is he to do?' He saw the ball go **merrily bouncing** down the street and then **merrily over**, into the water.

**The boy's grief:** the boy stands **rigid, trembling**, staring down **'all his young days'** into the harbour where his ball went. The ball is linked with the memories of his childhood days.

**No intrusion:** the poet says 'No use to say "O there are other balls"'. He **would not intrude** on the boy. He will not offer him **a dime** for another ball: it is worthless. The boy must learn, for the first time, the **responsibility** of possessing things in 'the world of possessions'.

**The lesson:** **'Balls will be lost always, little boy'**. Money is **external**: it cannot buy back what is truly lost. The boy is learning **'the epistemology of loss'**, that is, the nature of loss and how to stand up after it. Everyone has to learn this some day.

blocks.title: Key phrases
blocks.body:
| Phrase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **'merrily bouncing... merrily over'** | the ball's happy movement contrasts with the boy's sadness |
| **'staring down / All his young days'** | the ball holds the memories of his childhood |
| **'I would not intrude on him'** | the poet will not interfere; the boy must face this alone |
| **'the world of possessions'** | a world where we own things and must accept losing them |
| **'Money is external'** | money cannot replace feelings or memories |
| **'the epistemology of loss'** | knowing what loss means and how to bear it |

blocks.question: What does 'the epistemology of loss' mean?
options: understanding the nature of loss and how to cope with it
blocks.explanation: Epistemology is the study of knowledge.

blocks.question: Where did the boy's ball go?
blocks.explanation: It bounced down the street and then over into the water.
option_feedback: Into the water of the harbour.

blocks.title: How the poem works
blocks.body:
| Device | Example |
|---|---|
| **Repetition** | 'What, what is he to do?'; 'merrily... merrily' |
| **Enjambment** | lines run on, like the boy's flowing thoughts |
| **Free verse** | no regular rhyme scheme |
| **Symbolism** | the ball stands for childhood, and for everything we will lose in life |
| **Contrast** | 'merrily' bouncing ball vs the 'rigid, trembling' boy |

**Theme:** loss is part of life. We grow up when we learn to accept it and stand up again; no money can buy back what we have truly lost.

blocks.question: The ball in the poem symbolises:
options: childhood and the things we lose in life
blocks.explanation: The boy is learning about loss.
option_feedback: It is a symbol of loss.

blocks.title: Memory tricks
blocks.body:
- **Ball → harbour; boy rigid, trembling; poet won't intrude; money is external; balls will be lost always; epistemology of loss.**
- **Form: free verse.**

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
1. Thinking the poet is unkind: he lets the boy **learn** to bear loss.
2. Saying the boy will get another ball: the poet refuses to give money for one.
3. Thinking the poem is only about a ball: it is about **all loss**.

blocks.title: Try this in class
blocks.body: Ask students to describe something they lost and how they got over it, in five sentences.

blocks.title: Think and explain
blocks.body: Have you ever lost something you liked very much? How did you feel, and how did you get over it?

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body: - **Madam Rides the Bus and The Sermon at Benares:** first lessons in loss and death.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
'Balls will be lost always, little boy.' What lesson does the boy learn? Answer in about 120 words.

**Model answer:** The boy's ball, which he has had for a long time, bounces into the harbour. He stands rigid and trembling, staring at the water as if all his young days had gone with it, because the ball carried his childhood memories. The poet could buy him another ball, but he chooses not to intrude: a new ball would not replace what is lost, since 'money is external'. The boy is learning, for the first time, the responsibility of owning things in a world of possessions, where things will always be lost. He is learning 'the epistemology of loss', that is, how to understand loss and stand up again. This is a lesson every person must learn to grow up.

blocks.title: Summary
blocks.body:
- A boy loses his ball in the harbour and is deeply upset.
- The poet does not intrude or offer money for a new ball.
- The boy is learning that loss is part of life and must be borne: 'the epistemology of loss'.

blocks.title: Exam tips
blocks.body:
- Explain 'money is external' and 'epistemology of loss' in simple words.
- Show why the poet does not intrude.
- Link the ball to childhood and to life's other losses.

blocks.front: Why doesn't the poet buy the boy another ball?
blocks.back: The boy must learn to accept loss; money is external and cannot replace what is lost.
Understanding what loss is and how to stand up after it.
